title: Hector monet. Nox armata
titleEn: Hector's Warning and the Night Battle — Aeneid II.287–385
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Hector's ghost has no time for Aeneas's questions. Groaning from deep in his chest, he tells him to flee the burning city: Troy has given enough to Priam and the fatherland, and if any hand could have saved the citadel, this one would have; Troy now entrusts to him her sacred things and household gods, and he must seek great walls for them across the sea. The ghost carries out the fillets, Vesta and the undying fire from the inner shrine. The din grows; Anchises' house stands apart, screened by trees, but Aeneas wakes, climbs to the roof and listens like a shepherd on a crag who hears a flood or a wind-driven fire sweeping the crops. The truth is plain: Deiphobus's great house collapses, Ucalegon's burns next, and the straits of Sigeum glow. Aeneas snatches up arms with no plan, only the wish to gather a band and die fighting. Panthus, priest of Apollo, escapes the Greek spears with the conquered gods and his small grandson, and tells him that the last day has come: Troy has been, the horse pours out armed men, Sinon spreads fire, and as many Greeks as ever came from Mycenae hold the gates and the narrow ways. Carried on by the Fury and the shouting, Aeneas is joined by Rhipeus, Epytus, Hypanis, Dymas and young Coroebus, who had come to Troy for love of Cassandra and, unhappy man, ignored her frantic warnings. Aeneas tells them the gods have left, and that the one safety for the beaten is to hope for none. They go forth like wolves in a black mist through the weapons and the enemy, into the heart of the city. Night, slaughter and dread are everywhere; the Trojans die, and the Greeks too. Androgeos with a crowd of Greeks takes them for friends and calls them to hurry. He sees at once his mistake and starts back like a man who has trodden on a snake; Aeneas's band falls on the surprised Greeks and cuts them down, and Fortune seems to favour the start.
part: Hector's Warning and the Night Battle (II.287–385)

sentences.t:
Ille nihil, nec me quaerentem vana moratur,
sed graviter gemitus imo de pectore ducens,
“Heu fuge, nate dea, teque his, ait, eripe flammis.
sentences.l:
He nothing, nor me asking vain things delays,
but heavily groans from the deepest breast drawing,
“Alas flee, goddess-born, and yourself from these flames snatch.
sentences.i: He answers nothing, and heeds none of my idle questions, but draws deep groans heavily from the bottom of his chest: “Ah, flee, son of a goddess, and tear yourself from these flames.
sentences.n: Hector is the subject of the first verb; he is 'ille', the ghost of Hector seen in the dream of the previous part. 'nihil' is an adverbial accusative, 'in nothing, not at all', and 'moratur' is the deponent 'moror', 'delay, detain': he does not stop to indulge Aeneas's idle questions. 'quaerentem' is a present participle agreeing with 'me'. 'ducens' is also present participle, 'drawing' the groans up. A new speech opens at 289 inside the sentence: 'ait' is dropped into it. 'fuge' and 'eripe' are imperatives; 'nate' is the vocative of 'natus', and 'dea' is an ablative of origin, 'goddess-born' (Aeneas's mother is Venus). 'te… eripe' — 'eripio' with a reflexive object and the ablative 'flammis' of separation.

sentences.t: Hostis habet muros; ruit alto a culmine Troia.
sentences.l: The enemy holds the walls; falls from the high summit Troy.
sentences.i: The enemy has the walls; Troy is toppling from her high summit.
sentences.n: 'Hostis' is a collective singular, 'the enemy'. 'ruit' is a present tense for vividness, and 'alto a culmine' is 'from the high top' — the city as a building coming down. 'Troia' is nominative and comes last for weight.

sentences.t:
Sat patriae Priamoque datum: si Pergama dextra
defendi possent, etiam hac defensa fuissent.
sentences.l:
Enough to the fatherland and to Priam has been given: if Pergama by a right hand
could be defended, even by this it would have been defended.
sentences.i: Enough has been given to country and to Priam: if Pergama could be defended by any hand, it would have been defended by this one.
sentences.n: 'Sat' is 'satis'; 'datum' leaves out 'est'. 'patriae Priamoque' are datives of the persons for whom. 'Pergama' is a neuter plural, the citadel, used for Troy. The condition is mixed: 'si… possent' is an imperfect subjunctive (the present unreal) and 'defensa fuissent' a pluperfect (the past unreal): 'if it could be… it would have been'. 'hac' agrees with 'dextra' and means Hector's own right hand, the best defender Troy had.

sentences.t: Sacra suosque tibi commendat Troia penatis:
sentences.l: The holy things and her household gods to you entrusts Troy:
sentences.i: Troy hands to you her holy things and her household gods:
sentences.n: 'Sacra' is neuter plural, the sacred objects and rites. 'penatis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is for -es (you'll see this constantly). The 'penates' are the gods of the household and storeroom; Aeneas will carry them to Italy. The colon introduces the orders.

sentences.t:
hos cape fatorum comites, his moenia quaere
magna, pererrato statues quae denique ponto.”
sentences.l:
these take, companions of the fates, for these walls seek
great ones, which you will at last found, the sea having been wandered over.”
sentences.i: take them as the companions of your fate, and seek for them great walls, which you will found at last when you have wandered the whole sea.”
sentences.n: 'hos cape… his… quaere' — two imperatives; 'his' is a dative of advantage, 'for these'. 'fatorum comites' is genitive plural, 'companions in the fates'. 'quae' is a relative whose antecedent is 'moenia magna', 'statues' the second person singular future. 'pererrato ponto' is an ablative absolute, 'the sea having been traversed'. The speech closes here, as Greenough prints it, after the full stop.

sentences.t:
Sic ait, et manibus vittas Vestamque potentem
aeternumque adytis effert penetralibus ignem.
sentences.l:
So he speaks, and with his hands the fillets and powerful Vesta
and the everlasting fire carries out from the inner shrines.
sentences.i: So he speaks, and with his own hands carries out from the inner shrine the fillets, mighty Vesta and the undying fire.
sentences.n: 'Sic ait' is the usual formula of closing a speech. 'effert' (from 'effero', carry out) has three objects: 'vittas', 'Vestam' and 'ignem'. Vesta is the goddess of the hearth, whose perpetual fire was the sacred centre of a city; the fire of Troy's hearth passes to Aeneas, as Rome's would burn in the temple of Vesta. 'adytis… penetralibus' is an ablative of separation, 'from the inner sanctums'; 'adytum' is the Greek word for the unenterable inner room.

sentences.t:
Diverso interea miscentur moenia luctu,
et magis atque magis, quamquam secreta parentis
Anchisae domus arboribusque obtecta recessit,
clarescunt sonitus, armorumque ingruit horror.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile the city is confounded with grief in different directions,
and more and more, although apart my father
Anchises's house stood back and, covered by trees,
the sounds grow clear, and of arms the dread bears down.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the city is thrown into confusion, and grief runs in every direction; the noises grow plainer and plainer, though my father Anchises's house stood back, secluded and screened by trees, and the horror of arms comes bearing down on us.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'miscentur' is passive, 'is confused'; 'diverso luctu' an ablative of manner, 'with grief going several ways'. 'et magis atque magis' is 'more and more'. 'quamquam' takes the indicative here, 'recessit', 'withdrew, stood back'; 'secreta' and 'obtecta' agree with 'domus', 'secluded' and 'covered by'. 'parentis' is the genitive singular of 'parens' (father), and 'Anchisae' the genitive of a Greek name in -es (Anchises). 'ingruit' is the verb for a storm or force coming down on a thing; 'armorum… horror' is the clash and menace of arms.

sentences.t:
Excutior somno, et summi fastigia tecti
ascensu supero, atque arrectis auribus adsto:
sentences.l:
I am shaken from sleep, and of the highest roof the peak
I climb up by the ascent, and with ears pricked I stand:
sentences.i: I am shaken out of sleep, and by climbing I gain the topmost pitch of the roof, and stand with ears pricked:
sentences.n: 'Excutior' is a passive, 'I am shaken out of', the dream being broken. 'supero' with the accusative 'fastigia' means 'climb over, reach the top of'; 'ascensu' is an ablative of means, 'by climbing, by the way up'. 'arrectis auribus' is an ablative absolute, the pricked ears of a listening beast. 'adsto' is Greenough's spelling for 'asto' (Latin Library has 'asto'), the same verb. The colon leads into the long simile.

sentences.t:
in segetem veluti cum flamma furentibus austris
incidit, aut rapidus montano flumine torrens
sternit agros, sternit sata laeta boumque labores,
praecipitisque trahit silvas, stupet inscius alto
accipiens sonitum saxi de vertice pastor.
sentences.l:
as when on a crop with raging south winds a fire
falls, or a headlong torrent with a mountain stream
lays low the fields, lays low the glad crops and the labours of oxen,
and headlong drags the woods, the shepherd stunned, not knowing, from a high
crag's top taking in the sound.
sentences.i: as when fire falls on a cornfield with the south winds raging, or a rushing torrent from a mountain stream flattens the fields, flattens the happy crops and the labour of the oxen, and sweeps the forests headlong, and the shepherd, unknowing, stands amazed, taking in the noise from the top of a high rock.
sentences.n: A double simile, fire and flood, in the manner of Homer's (compare the Iliad's similes of forest fire and winter torrent); both ruin the farmer's work. 'in segetem… incidit' — 'falls on the standing grain'. 'furentibus austris' is an ablative absolute, 'the south winds raging'. 'sternit' is repeated for effect. 'boumque labores' — 'the labours of the oxen' for the ploughed and harvested fields, a poetic periphrasis. 'praecipitis' is most naturally an accusative plural agreeing with 'silvas', 'headlong' (some take it as the torrent's own epithet). 'stupet inscius' — the shepherd, who does not know the cause, is struck dumb. 'accipiens' is a present participle, 'receiving' the sound; 'de vertice' is 'from the top'. The point of the comparison is that Aeneas, on the roof, listens as the shepherd does, unable to see the thing that is coming.

sentences.t:
Tum vero manifesta fides, Danaumque patescunt
insidiae.
sentences.l:
Then indeed the proof is plain, and of the Danaans lie open
the snares.
sentences.i: Then indeed the proof is clear, and the Greeks' ambush lies open to view.
sentences.n: 'manifesta fides' — 'the proof is manifest', with 'est' left out. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural in -um (you'll see this constantly). 'patescunt' is inchoative (-sco), 'become open'. 'insidiae' is the 'snares', the ambush of the horse.

sentences.t:
Iam Deiphobi dedit ampla ruinam
Volcano superante domus;
sentences.l:
Already of Deiphobus the spacious house has given collapse,
Vulcan overpowering;
sentences.i: Already the roomy house of Deiphobus has crashed down before the conquering fire;
sentences.n: 'dedit ruinam' is 'gave (a) collapse, fell in ruin'. 'Volcano superante' is an ablative absolute: Vulcan, god of fire, stands for fire itself (metonymy). 'ampla domus' is the nominative, spaced round the verb. Deiphobus is a son of Priam, and the poem will show him killed that night.

sentences.t:
iam proxumus ardet
Ucalegon;
sentences.l:
already the next burns,
Ucalegon;
sentences.i: already the next house, Ucalegon's, is ablaze;
sentences.n: 'proxumus' is Greenough's spelling of 'proximus' (Latin Library has 'proximus'), 'next, nearest'. 'Ucalegon' is the name of an elder of Troy (he is named among the Trojan elders in the Iliad), here standing for his house: the owner's name for the thing owned (metonymy).

sentences.t: Sigea igni freta lata relucent.
sentences.l: the Sigean straits wide with fire gleam back.
sentences.i: the wide Sigean waters shine back with the flames.
sentences.n: 'Sigea freta lata' is a neuter plural subject; 'Sigeum' was the headland on the Trojan coast at the mouth of the Hellespont. 'igni' is an ablative of means, 'with fire'. 'relucent' is 'gleam back': the burning city is reflected on the water. The 'freta' (straits) are plural.

sentences.t: Exoritur clamorque virum clangorque tubarum.
sentences.l: There rises the shout of men and the blare of trumpets.
sentences.i: The shouting of men goes up, and the blare of trumpets.
sentences.n: 'Exoritur' is a present tense, singular, with the two subjects 'clamor' and 'clangor' following it, the verb agreeing with the nearer. 'virum' is the old genitive plural (for 'virorum'); the pairing 'clamor-que… clangor-que' is the double 'que' (you'll see this constantly).

sentences.t: Arma amens capio;
sentences.l: Arms, senseless, I seize;
sentences.i: Out of my mind, I seize my arms;
sentences.n: 'amens' means 'out of his mind', in a panic; it is the nominative adjective of the speaker, Aeneas, and sets the tone of the next lines: 'furor' is not the cool courage of the hero. The semicolon starts the explanation: 'for there is not enough reason in arms'.

sentences.i: nor is there reason enough in arms; but my spirit burns to gather a band for the fight and rush with my comrades to the citadel;
sentences.n: 'nec sat rationis' — 'sat' is 'satis', 'enough', followed by a partitive genitive ('rationis', 'of reason'). 'ardent animi' takes the infinitives 'glomerare' and 'concurrere', 'burn to gather… and to run together'; 'bello' is best taken as a dative of purpose, 'for the war' (it could also be read as an ablative). 'animi' is plural, 'my spirits'. 'arcem' is the citadel, Troy's high stronghold.

sentences.t:
furor iraque mentem
praecipitant, pulchrumque mori succurrit in armis.
sentences.l:
fury and anger my mind
hurl headlong, and it is a fine thing to die in arms comes to mind.
sentences.i: fury and rage drive my mind headlong, and the thought comes to me that it is fine to die in arms.
sentences.n: Greenough prints 'praecipitant' (plural, agreeing with both 'furor' and 'ira'); the Latin Library has 'praecipitat' (singular, agreeing with the nearer subject). Either is possible, since a verb with two subjects can take the plural; the sense is the same. 'praecipito' is here transitive, 'throw headlong'. 'pulchrumque mori' — 'pulchrum mori' ('to die is fine': a neuter adjective used as a noun, with an infinitive) is itself the subject of 'succurrit', 'occurs to me'; no 'est' is needed. 'in armis' is 'in arms'.

sentences.t:
Ecce autem telis Panthus elapsus Achivom,
Panthus Othryades, arcis Phoebique sacerdos,
sacra manu victosque deos parvumque nepotem
ipse trahit, cursuque amens ad limina tendit.
sentences.l:
Behold, however, out of the Achaeans' weapons slipped away Panthus,
Panthus, Othrys's son, of the citadel and of Phoebus the priest,
holy things in hand, and the conquered gods, and his little grandson
himself drags, and in a run, senseless, to the threshold makes his way.
sentences.i: And now Panthus, son of Othrys, priest of the citadel and of Phoebus, has slipped out through the Greek weapons, and himself drags along the holy things, the conquered gods and his little grandson, and distracted, hurries running toward my door.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'elapsus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'elabor', 'having slipped away', with 'telis' an ablative of separation; 'Achivom' is the old genitive plural in -om (Latin Library prints 'Achiuum'): you'll see this constantly. 'Othryades' is a patronymic, 'son of Othrys' (a Greek form). Panthus (the Greek Panthous) is a priest of Apollo ('Phoebus') in the citadel: his 'victos deos' are the images of the gods now beaten with Troy. 'ipse trahit' — he drags the child himself. 'cursu' is an ablative of manner; 'amens' is nominative.

sentences.t: “Quo res summa, loco, Panthu?
sentences.l: “In what place is the main matter, Panthus?
sentences.i: “Where does the great issue stand, Panthus?
sentences.n: The speech is Aeneas's. 'Quo… loco' is ablative of place, 'in what position'; 'res summa' is the main issue, 'the state of things'; 'est' is understood. 'Panthu' is a Greek vocative: the name is Greek (Panthoos), and its vocative ends in -u; a Latin second-declension name in -us would have -e.

sentences.t: Quam prendimus arcem?”
sentences.l: What citadel do we seize?”
sentences.i: What stronghold are we to hold?”
sentences.n: 'prendimus' is the syncopated form of 'prehendimus', 'seize, take hold of', in the present indicative. 'arcem' is the object, 'stronghold'. Greenough prints the closing mark after the question mark.

sentences.t: Vix ea fatus eram, gemitu cum talia reddit:
sentences.l: Scarcely these things had I said, when with a groan such things he replies:
sentences.i: Hardly had I said this when he answers with a groan:
sentences.n: 'fatus eram' is a pluperfect of the deponent 'for, fari' (a perfect passive form with an active sense). 'Vix… cum' takes the pluperfect in the main clause (the 'cum inversum'), the main action coming second. 'reddit' is a historic present.

sentences.t:
“Venit summa dies et ineluctabile tempus
Dardaniae:
sentences.l:
“Has come the last day and the inescapable time
of Dardania:
sentences.i: “The final day has come, the hour that cannot be escaped, for Dardania:
sentences.n: 'summa dies' is 'the last day'. 'ineluctabile' is neuter, agreeing with 'tempus': 'that cannot be struggled out of'. 'Dardaniae' is a genitive singular (Dardania, the land of Dardanus, i.e., Troy). The colon introduces the explanation: 'fuimus Troes…'.

sentences.t:
fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium et ingens
gloria Teucrorum;
sentences.l:
we have been Trojans, there has been Ilium and the huge
glory of the Teucrians;
sentences.i: we Trojans have been, Ilium has been, and the great glory of the Teucrians;
sentences.n: 'fuimus Troes, fuit Ilium' — the perfect of 'sum' used as 'we are no more' is a phrase of finality, often said of the dead ('fuit' = 'is no longer'). 'Troes' is a Greek nominative plural; 'Teucrorum' a genitive plural. 'et' joins 'Ilium' and 'gloria' (the city's glory also gone).

sentences.t:
ferus omnia Iuppiter Argos
transtulit;
sentences.l:
cruel Jupiter all things to Argos
has carried over;
sentences.i: cruel Jupiter has carried everything over to Argos;
sentences.n: 'ferus' is the nominative adjective of Jupiter, 'savage'. 'omnia Argos transtulit' — 'omnia' is the object, and 'Argos' is the place to which, in the accusative without a preposition (as with names of towns). 'transtulit' is the perfect of 'transfero', 'has transferred': Jupiter has turned the fortune of the war to the Greeks.

sentences.t: incensa Danai dominantur in urbe.
sentences.l: in the burning city the Danaans are lords.
sentences.i: the Greeks are masters in a city set on fire.
sentences.n: 'in urbe' is the place, and the participle 'incensa' agrees with 'urbe': 'in a city set on fire'. 'Danai' is a nominative plural; 'dominantur' is a deponent verb, 'are masters'.

sentences.i: The tall horse, standing in the middle of the walls, pours out armed men, and Sinon, the victor, stirs the fires together, exulting;
sentences.n: 'Arduus equus' — the adjective 'arduus' (steep, towering) and the noun are placed at the two ends of the clause, with the armed men in between, as the horse holds them. 'adstans' is Greenough's spelling of 'astans' (Latin Library 'astans'). 'armatos' is used as a noun, 'armed men'. 'fundit' means 'pours out'. 'victor Sinon' — Sinon, the lying prisoner of the previous part, now triumphs; 'insultans' is a present participle, 'leaping on, exulting'. 'incendia miscet' — 'mixes fires' means 'sets fire in all places'.

sentences.t:
portis alii bipatentibus adsunt,
milia quot magnis umquam venere Mycenis;
sentences.l:
at the gates, with their double-opening, others are present,
thousands as many as ever came from great Mycenae;
sentences.i: others stand at the wide double gates, as many thousands as ever came from great Mycenae;
sentences.n: 'portis… bipatentibus' is an ablative of place ('at the gates'), 'bipatentibus' meaning 'opening both ways' (two leaves). 'alii' begins the series 'alii… alii'. 'milia quot' is a relative clause of quantity, 'as many thousands as'; 'venere' = 'venerunt' (the -ere ending, you'll see this constantly). 'Mycenis' is an ablative of source, 'from Mycenae', without a preposition (Mycenae, Agamemnon's city, is plural in Latin).

sentences.t:
obsedere alii telis angusta viarum
oppositi;
sentences.l:
have beset others with weapons the narrow parts of the streets,
set in the way;
sentences.i: others have blocked the narrow places of the streets, drawn up across them with their weapons;
sentences.n: 'obsedere' = 'obsederunt' (the -ere ending). 'angusta viarum' — 'angusta' is a neuter plural used as a noun with the partitive genitive 'viarum', 'the narrow parts of the streets'. 'oppositi' is a nominative plural masculine agreeing with 'alii'; the Latin Library prints 'oppositis', which would agree with 'telis' ('with weapons set against'); the sense is nearly the same. 'telis' is an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
stat ferri acies mucrone corusco
stricta, parata neci;
sentences.l:
stands of steel the edge, with a flashing point,
drawn, ready for slaughter;
sentences.i: the edge of steel stands drawn, its point gleaming, ready for slaughter;
sentences.n: 'ferri acies' — 'acies' is the edge or line, 'ferri' the genitive 'of iron' (so, 'a battle line of iron' or 'a sword's edge'; the two readings run together). 'stricta' agrees with 'acies': 'strictus' is the participle of 'stringo', 'drawn'. 'mucrone corusco' is an ablative of quality, 'with a gleaming point'. 'neci' is a dative of purpose, 'for slaughter'.

sentences.t:
vix primi proelia temptant
portarum vigiles, et caeco Marte resistunt.”
sentences.l:
scarcely the first the guards of the gates attempt battles,
and in blind Mars resist.”
sentences.i: scarcely do the guards at the gates make their first try at battle, and they withstand in a blind fight.”
sentences.n: 'primi… vigiles portarum' — the first watchmen on the gates, who tried to stop them. 'caeco Marte' is an ablative of manner, 'in a blind fight' (Mars the god of war stands for fighting; 'blind' because the night hides the enemy). 'temptant' is the alternative spelling of 'tentant'. Greenough closes the speech here, after the full stop.

sentences.t:
Talibus Othryadae dictis et numine divom
in flammas et in arma feror, quo tristis Erinys,
quo fremitus vocat et sublatus ad aethera clamor.
sentences.l:
By such words of Othrys's son and the will of the gods
I am borne into flames and into arms, where the grim Fury,
where the uproar calls and the shout raised to the sky.
sentences.i: Moved by the words of Othrys's son and the will of the gods, I am borne into the flames and into the fighting, where the grim Fury calls me, where the uproar calls and the cry lifted to the sky.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Talibus Othryadae dictis' — 'Othryadae' is the Greek genitive singular (of Othryades, Panthus); 'dictis' is an ablative of cause or means. 'divom' is the old genitive plural (for 'divorum'), Greenough's spelling (Latin Library 'diuum'): the gods' will, the 'numen', sweeps Aeneas on. 'feror' is a passive, 'I am carried', not 'I go'. 'quo… quo' is the relative adverb 'to where' repeated, and 'vocat' is singular with a run of subjects. 'Erinys' is the Greek Fury (nominative singular); 'sublatus' is a participle of 'tollo'.

sentences.t:
Addunt se socios Rhipeus et maximus armis
Epytus oblati per lunam Hypanisque Dymasque,
et lateri adglomerant nostro, iuvenisque Coroebus,
Mygdonides:
sentences.l:
Join themselves as allies Rhipeus and greatest in arms
Epytus, offered by the moon, and Hypanis and Dymas,
and to our side they crowd, and the youth Coroebus,
Mygdon's son:
sentences.i: Rhipeus joins me, and Epytus, greatest in arms, and Hypanis and Dymas, all brought into view by the moon; they crowd to our side, and with them young Coroebus, the son of Mygdon.
sentences.n: 'Addunt se socios' — 'they add themselves as allies'. Rhipeus, Epytus, Hypanis and Dymas are minor Trojans (Rhipeus is called the most just of the Trojans in line 426). 'maximus armis' is an ablative of respect, 'greatest in arms'. 'oblati' is a perfect passive participle of 'offero', 'presented to us'. 'per lunam' means 'by the light of the moon'. 'adglomerant' is Greenough's spelling of 'agglomerant', with the dative 'lateri nostro'. 'Mygdonides' is a patronymic in apposition to 'Coroebus'. The colon starts the explanation of how he came to Troy.

sentences.t:
illis ad Troiam forte diebus
venerat, insano Cassandrae incensus amore,
et gener auxilium Priamo Phrygibusque ferebat,
infelix, qui non sponsae praecepta furentis
audierit.
sentences.l:
in those days, by chance, to Troy
had come, burning with mad love of Cassandra,
and as son-in-law help to Priam and the Phrygians was bringing,
unlucky, who the warnings of his betrothed,
raving, did not hear.
sentences.i: he had come to Troy by chance in those days, set on fire by a mad passion for Cassandra, and as a son-in-law was bringing help to Priam and the Phrygians, unlucky man, since he did not listen to the warnings of his raving bride.
sentences.n: 'illis diebus' is an ablative of time. 'insano… amore' is an ablative of cause, 'with mad love'. 'gener' is in apposition to the subject, 'as son-in-law (to be)'. 'Phrygibus' is a dative, the Phrygians being the Trojans. 'infelix' is a nominative standing alone. 'qui… audierit' is a relative clause of characteristic with a causal sense, 'seeing that he was one who did not heed'; it uses a perfect subjunctive to state a completed fact, as characteristic and result clauses may even after a past tense like 'ferebat'. 'audierit' is Virgil's unfinished line: Greenough prints it as a half-line (hemistich), and the next line begins afresh. 'sponsae… furentis' are genitives, 'of his raving betrothed'. Cassandra, Priam's daughter, had the gift of prophecy and the curse of never being believed.

sentences.t:
Quos ubi confertos audere in proelia vidi,
incipio super his:
sentences.l:
These, when I saw them massed, to dare for battles,
I begin, over and above this:
sentences.i: When I saw them closely drawn together and bold for the fight, I began, adding this:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Quos' is a connecting relative. 'ubi' with the perfect 'vidi' means 'when I saw'. 'audere' (Greenough; the Latin Library has 'ardere') is the infinitive after 'vidi' with 'quos' as its subject: 'saw them to dare'. 'ardere' would read 'burn for battle'; the sense differs a little (dare, as against burn), but both fit the picture; Greenough's 'audere' is followed here. 'confertos' is a participle, 'crowded together'. 'incipio' with the ellipsis of 'dicere' ('I begin (to speak)'), in the historic present. 'super his' is 'on top of this, in addition'.

sentences.t:
“Iuvenes, fortissima frustra
pectora, si vobis audentem extrema cupido
certa sequi, quae sit rebus fortuna videtis:
sentences.l:
“Young men, bravest in vain
hearts, if to you, me daring the last things, a desire
sure to follow, what fortune there is for our affairs you see:
sentences.i: “Young men, hearts brave to no purpose, if your desire is set to follow one who dares the last extreme, you see how fortune stands for us:
sentences.n: The speech opens here in the middle of line 348. 'fortissima… pectora' is a vocative, the 'bravest hearts', with 'frustra' (to no purpose). 'si vobis… cupido certa' — the dative of possession ('est' is left out), 'if you have a fixed desire'. 'audentem' is a present participle in the accusative, agreeing with an unwritten 'me': 'following me who dare'. 'extrema' is a neuter plural noun, 'the last things'. 'quae sit rebus fortuna' is an indirect question with 'sit' in the subjunctive; 'rebus' is a dative, 'for the state of affairs'.

sentences.t:
excessere omnes, adytis arisque relictis,
di, quibus imperium hoc steterat;
sentences.l:
gone out are all, the shrines and altars having been left,
the gods by whom this empire had stood;
sentences.i: all the gods by whom this empire had stood are gone, forsaking shrine and altar;
sentences.n: 'excessere' = 'excesserunt'. 'adytis arisque relictis' is an ablative absolute, 'the shrines and altars abandoned'. The gods leaving a doomed city was a regular ancient belief. 'quibus… steterat' — the pluperfect, 'had stood', 'quibus' being an ablative of means or support, 'on whom this empire had rested' (the god-based standing of the state).

sentences.t:
succurritis urbi
incensae;
sentences.l:
you come to the aid of a city
burning;
sentences.i: you are helping a city that is on fire;
sentences.n: 'succurritis' is the present indicative, 'you are coming to the help of' (with the dative 'urbi'). The sense is that it is already too late: 'a burning city' has nothing left to save.

sentences.t: moriamur et in media arma ruamus.
sentences.l: let us die and rush into the midst of arms.
sentences.i: let us die, and let us rush into the thick of the fight.
sentences.n: 'moriamur' and 'ruamus' are present subjunctives, hortatory ('let us'); 'moriamur' is the deponent 'morior'. The two verbs fall on the same line. 'media arma' is 'the midst of the arms'.

sentences.t: Una salus victis, nullam sperare salutem.”
sentences.l: One safety to the conquered, to hope for no safety.”
sentences.i: For men defeated there is one hope of safety: to look for none.”
sentences.n: A famous paradox. 'Una salus' is the subject, 'victis' the dative of the people, 'nullam sperare salutem' the infinitive phrase in apposition ('to hope for no safety'). The line is a rhetorical flourish. The speech ends at the end of the line.

sentences.t: Sic animis iuvenum furor additus:
sentences.l: So to the spirits of the young men fury was added:
sentences.i: So rage was added to the young men's courage:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'animis iuvenum' is a dative, 'to the spirits of the youths'. 'furor additus' is the passive participle, the verb 'est' omitted. The colon introduces the simile and what follows.

sentences.t:
inde, lupi ceu
raptores atra in nebula, quos improba ventris
exegit caecos rabies, catulique relicti
faucibus exspectant siccis,
sentences.l:
then, as wolves
ravening in black mist, whom the wicked madness of the belly
has driven out blind, and the cubs, left,
wait with dry throats,
sentences.i: then, like ravening wolves in a black mist, whom the cruel rage of the belly has driven out blind, while the cubs they left behind wait with parched throats,
sentences.n: 'inde' marks the next stage. 'lupi ceu raptores' — the simile begins with 'ceu', 'like'; 'raptores' is a noun in apposition, 'robbers, ravenous ones'. Wolf-similes for men going out to battle are Homeric (compare the wolves of the Iliad). 'quos improba ventris… rabies exegit caecos' — 'exegit' is the perfect of 'exigo', 'has driven out'; 'caecos' agrees with 'quos', 'blind' with hunger and in the dark. 'faucibus… siccis' is an ablative of description, 'with dry jaws'. The unit ends at a comma, since the sentence runs on.

sentences.i: so through weapons and through foes we go to a death that is certain, and keep the road to the middle of the city;
sentences.n: The main clause of the simile: 'vadimus'. 'haud dubiam in mortem' — 'haud dubiam' means 'not doubtful', a litotes for 'certain'. 'mediae… urbis iter' — 'mediae' (agreeing with 'urbis') is in the other line from its noun: 'the way of the mid-city'. 'tenemus' is 'we hold (to), keep'. 'hostis' is Greenough's accusative plural in -is (you'll see this constantly).

sentences.t: nox atra cava circumvolat umbra.
sentences.l: black night flies around with hollow shade.
sentences.i: black night wheels about us in a hollow shadow.
sentences.n: 'cava umbra' is an ablative of manner, the shadow 'hollow' like a vault; 'circumvolat' is 'flies around', night pictured as a winged thing hovering about them. The sentence is a short description.

sentences.t:
Quis cladem illius noctis, quis funera fando
explicet, aut possit lacrimis aequare labores?
sentences.l:
Who the slaughter of that night, who the deaths in telling
could unfold, or could with tears match the labours?
sentences.i: Who, by telling, could lay out the slaughter of that night, who its deaths, or match its sufferings with tears?
sentences.n: 'Quis… explicet aut possit' — two present subjunctives in a rhetorical question (potential, 'who could…?'). 'fando' is the ablative of the gerund, 'by telling'. 'lacrimis' is an ablative of means. The question, with 'aequare', 'make equal', says that the grief of that night is greater than any tears. 'cladem' and 'funera' are the objects of 'explicet'.

sentences.t: Urbs antiqua ruit, multos dominata per annos;
sentences.l: The ancient city falls, having ruled through many years;
sentences.i: The old city is falling, after ruling for many years;
sentences.n: 'dominata' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'dominor' used actively, 'having been mistress'. 'multos per annos' — the preposition sits between adjective and noun.

sentences.t:
plurima perque vias sternuntur inertia passim
corpora, perque domos et religiosa deorum
limina.
sentences.l:
very many through the streets are laid low, inert,
bodies, and through homes and the gods' holy
thresholds.
sentences.i: Throughout the streets lie countless bodies strewn limp, and through the houses, and across the holy thresholds of the gods.
sentences.n: 'plurima… corpora' is the subject, 'inertia' (without movement) agreeing; 'sternuntur' is a passive (the sense: 'are strewn'). 'perque… perque' repeats the preposition with the double 'que' (you'll see this constantly). 'religiosa… limina' — 'religiosus' means 'holy, bound by the sacred'; the dead lie even in the temples. 'deorum' is the genitive plural.

sentences.t: Nec soli poenas dant sanguine Teucri;
sentences.l: Nor alone penalties give with blood the Teucrians;
sentences.i: Nor are the Trojans alone in paying with their blood;
sentences.n: 'Nec soli… Teucri' — 'soli' is a plural nominative adjective, the Trojans 'alone'. 'poenas dant' is the idiom for 'pay the penalty'; 'sanguine' is an ablative of means, 'with blood'. The semicolon leads to the contrast.

sentences.t:
quondam etiam victis redit in praecordia virtus
victoresque cadunt Danai:
sentences.l:
at times even to the conquered returns into the heart valour,
and the victors fall, the Danaans:
sentences.i: at times courage comes back into the hearts of the beaten too, and the victorious Greeks fall:
sentences.n: 'quondam' here is 'at times' (the sense it has when joined with a present). 'victis' is a dative of the person, 'to the conquered'; 'praecordia' is a neuter plural, the 'heart' (the parts in front of the heart). 'victores… Danai' — 'victores' is a noun in the nominative plural, with 'Danai' in apposition. The colon introduces a summary.

sentences.t:
crudelis ubique
luctus, ubique pavor, et plurima mortis imago.
sentences.l:
cruel everywhere
grief, everywhere dread, and very many a shape of death.
sentences.i: everywhere cruel grief, everywhere terror, and death in a thousand shapes.
sentences.n: 'crudelis ubique luctus' — the adjective is placed before 'ubique'; the first 'ubique' is repeated at the head of the second phrase (anaphora). 'plurima mortis imago' — 'plurima' is a superlative used for 'very many', 'imago' is singular for 'form'. There is no verb: 'est' is left out.

sentences.t:
Primus se, Danaum magna comitante caterva,
Androgeos offert nobis, socia agmina credens
inscius, atque ultro verbis compellat amicis:
sentences.l:
First himself, of the Danaans a great band accompanying,
Androgeos presents to us, our allied ranks believing,
unknowing, and unprompted with words friendly addresses:
sentences.i: First, with a great crowd of Greeks in his train, Androgeos offers himself to us, in ignorance thinking us a friendly column, and of his own accord greets us in friendly words:
sentences.n: A new paragraph. 'Primus se… offert' — 'Primus' is nominative where English would say 'first' as an adverb. 'Danaum' is the old genitive plural. 'comitante caterva' is an ablative absolute. 'Androgeos' is a Greek name, a nominative in -os. 'socia agmina credens inscius' — 'credens' takes 'socia agmina' as its object, with 'nos' and 'esse' understood: believing us (to be) friendly columns; 'inscius' is a nominative, 'not knowing'. 'ultro' means 'unprompted, of his own accord'. 'compellat' is 'accosts'.

sentences.t: “Festinate, viri:
sentences.l: “Hurry, men:
sentences.i: “Hurry, men:
sentences.n: 'Festinate' is a plural imperative; 'viri' is a vocative plural. A mark opens the speech of Androgeos. He is speaking to Aeneas's band, whom he takes for the other Greeks.

sentences.t:
nam quae tam sera moratur
segnities?
sentences.l:
for what so late
sluggishness delays you?
sentences.i: for what sluggishness so late holds you back?
sentences.n: 'nam quae… segnities' — 'quae' is the interrogative adjective agreeing with 'segnities'; the object 'vos' is left out. 'tam sera' — 'sera' is an adjective with the sense of an adverb, 'so late'. 'moratur' is the deponent verb, 'delays'.

sentences.t:
Alii rapiunt incensa feruntque
Pergama;
sentences.l:
Others plunder and carry off the burning
Pergama;
sentences.i: Others are plundering and carrying off burning Pergama;
sentences.n: 'rapiunt… feruntque' — 'rapere' and 'ferre' are a pair, 'to seize and carry off', the fixed phrase for looting. 'incensa' is an adjective in the same neuter plural as 'Pergama'.

sentences.t: vos celsis nunc primum a navibus itis.”
sentences.l: you from the lofty ships only now first come.”
sentences.i: you are only now coming from the high ships.”
sentences.n: 'celsis a navibus' — the preposition sits between its adjective and noun; 'a' is 'from'. 'nunc primum' is 'just now for the first time'. The closing mark follows the full stop, as Greenough prints it.

sentences.t:
Dixit, et extemplo, neque enim responsa dabantur
fida satis, sensit medios delapsus in hostis.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and at once, for answers were not given
trustworthy enough, he perceived, having fallen into the midst of foes.
sentences.i: He had spoken, and at once, since the answers given him were not trustworthy enough, he understood that he had slipped into the middle of the enemy.
sentences.n: 'Dixit' is a perfect. 'extemplo' is 'immediately'. 'neque enim… dabantur' — 'neque' is 'not' (as 'non'), 'for the answers were not being given trustworthy enough'; the imperfect passive is the sign that the answers, that is Aeneas's men's replies, did not inspire confidence. 'fida' is a neuter plural agreeing with 'responsa'. 'delapsus' is the perfect participle of the deponent 'delabor' (active sense), 'having slipped down'; 'medios… hostis' (accusative plural in -is, 'the middle of the enemies').

sentences.t: Obstipuit, retroque pedem cum voce repressit:
sentences.l: He was struck dumb, and backward his foot with his voice checked:
sentences.i: He froze, and held back both foot and voice:
sentences.n: 'Obstipuit' is the perfect of 'obstipesco', 'was stupefied'. 'retro' is an adverb of 'back'; 'repressit' is 'checked'. The sense is that he stopped speaking and stepped back at one moment. The colon starts the simile.

sentences.i: like a man who in his path has trodden on an unseen snake among the rough brambles, and suddenly, shaking, shrinks back from it as it lifts its anger and swells its dark-blue neck;
sentences.n: A simile of a snake underfoot; compare the Iliad, where Paris shrinks back from Menelaus like a man who has stepped on a snake. 'inprovisum' is Greenough's spelling of 'improvisum', 'unseen, not foreseen', agreeing with 'anguem'. 'veluti qui… pressit' — 'qui' is 'he who', with the perfect indicative. 'humi nitens' — 'humi' is a locative, 'on the ground', and 'nitens' (from 'nitor') 'treading, pressing'. 'attollentem iras' and 'caerula colla tumentem' are present participles in the accusative agreeing with 'anguem'; 'colla' is a Greek-style accusative of respect, 'swelling as to its neck'. 'iras' is plural (a poetic plural, 'anger').

sentences.t: haud secus Androgeos visu tremefactus abibat.
sentences.l: not otherwise Androgeos, by the sight trembling, was going away.
sentences.i: just so Androgeos, shaken at the sight of us, drew away.
sentences.n: The point of the comparison. 'haud secus' is 'not otherwise, just so'. 'visu' is the ablative of the fourth-declension noun 'visus', 'sight', here of cause: 'at the sight' (not a supine). 'tremefactus' is a perfect participle of 'tremefacio', 'caused to tremble'. 'abibat' is imperfect, he was starting away.

sentences.t:
Inruimus, densis et circumfundimur armis,
ignarosque loci passim et formidine captos
sternimus:
sentences.l:
We rush in, and with dense arms are poured around them,
and the ignorant of the place everywhere and by fear taken
we lay low:
sentences.i: We rush upon them and pour round them in close array, and strike down, all about, men who do not know the ground and are seized with terror:
sentences.n: 'Inruimus' is Greenough's spelling of 'irruimus'. 'circumfundimur' is a passive in the sense of a middle, 'we pour ourselves round'. 'ignaros loci' — 'ignarus' takes a genitive, 'unaware of the place'; 'formidine captos' is 'seized by fear', an ablative of cause. 'passim' is 'here and there, all over'. The Greeks, in strange streets at night, are the ones at a disadvantage. The colon leads to the verdict.

sentences.t: adspirat primo fortuna labori.
sentences.l: favours with its breath the first effort Fortune.
sentences.i: Fortune breathes kindly on our first attempt.
sentences.n: 'adspirat' is Greenough's spelling of 'aspirat', 'breathes toward, favours' (the word is used of a wind that helps a ship). 'primo labori' is a dative, 'for the first labour'. 'fortuna' follows its verb and dative at the end. The brief success will turn bad in the next part.
